analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal bureau to cap drug prices, forces price rebates above inflation, and lets Medicare negotiate drug prices.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate health committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a new federal bureau that reviews what drug companies charge, declares some prices excessive, and forces manufacturers to cut them or pay back the difference to patients. It would cap prices of top-selling brand-name drugs at what other developed countries pay, require companies to disclose research, marketing, and profit data for every drug, let Medicare negotiate prices for the first time, and let the government license a drug's patents to competitors if a company refuses to lower an unjustified price. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who fills a prescription, especially Medicare beneficiaries and patients on expensive brand-name drugs with no generic competition. The bill caps prices at the median of what eleven other developed countries pay, forces rebates when prices rise faster than inflation (with the money returned to affected patients), and authorizes Medicare to negotiate. It also gives patients a formal channel to petition for a review of any drug they find unaffordable.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and taxpayers paying drug prices

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Bureau of Prescription Drug Affordability and Access that must review drug prices and cap any price it finds excessive, with patients able to petition for a review of a drug they cannot afford.

Sets an interim ceiling on prices of brand-name drugs without generic competition at the median list price in eleven other developed countries, including Canada, the United Kingdom, France, Germany, and Japan.
Requires manufacturers that raise prices faster than inflation to justify the increase, and any unjustified excess is treated as 'excess revenue' that must be rebated to patients who overpaid.
Repeals the 'non-interference clause' that bars Medicare from negotiating drug prices, and allows the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to negotiate.

As an enforcement backstop, if a manufacturer refuses to lower an unjustified price or pay back excess revenue, the government can authorize competitors to make the drug using the manufacturer's patents and government-granted exclusivities, with compensation set by the government.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose revenues would fall under price caps, foreign-reference benchmarks, inflation rebates, and the threat of forced patent licensing; also taxpayers, who fund the new $50 million-a-year bureau.

drawbacks.text: The bill lets a federal bureau override a drug's list price and, as a last resort, license its patents to competitors, which manufacturers argue would reduce incentives to invest in developing new medicines and could slow innovation.

Tying allowed U.S. prices to the median list prices of eleven foreign reference countries imports those countries' pricing policies, and manufacturers would face penalties of 150 percent of excess revenues while the Bureau's judgments about an 'appropriate' price rest on discretionary factors.

The bill would create a new $50 million-per-year federal bureau and extensive mandatory corporate disclosure, an administrative expansion some would view as unnecessary government intrusion into private pricing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit — international-reference pricing, mandatory rebates, patent-marching-in as enforcement, and Medicare negotiation — is one of the strongest price-control designs proposed in recent Congresses, and the disclosure requirements would also force real transparency. The honest costs are real: hard price caps and forced generic licensing could reduce manufacturers' incentive to invest in high-risk research, and manufacturers would inevitably argue that capping prices based on other countries' systems (many of which impose their own controls) shifts too much risk. But because the bill never advanced, none of these trade-offs were ever tested in debate — the cost to the public is that nothing happened at all.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Health Committee on the same day and no further action was ever taken before the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on January 8, 2020.
It was read twice and referred the same day to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
That is the last action of any kind: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no companion action before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers keep the current pricing system — no price bureau, no foreign-reference caps, no patient rebates, and no Medicare negotiation — and patients keep paying the resulting prices.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers and their investors

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 8, 2020 and took no action on the bill for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: Has long opposed price-setting and government negotiation measures of this kind, and industry opposition is widely credited with keeping such bills from advancing.

sides.party_line_note: Only three senators were attached to the bill (two Democrats and one Independent); no Republicans signed on and no vote was ever held, so no partisan split in support or opposition is measurable in the record.

industries.note: The bill subjects them to mandatory disclosure of R&D, marketing, and profit data, caps prices at foreign medians for top-selling drugs, forces rebates on above-inflation increases, and lets the government license their patents if they refuse to cut prices. It targets exactly the segment of the industry that relies on monopoly pricing.
The bill requires disclosure of the net prices PBMs realize after rebates, exposing the spread between list prices and what insurers and patients actually pay.
They could gain by being authorized to make drugs whose patents the government opens up, but the disclosed price information could also squeeze margins across the market.
